chapter_title: Understanding Scene Organization and Basic Objects
chapter_summary:
Now that you're comfortable navigating Maya's interface, let's start populating our 3D world. Every 3D scene in Maya is essentially a collection of objects, lights, cameras, and other elements that collectively form your virtual environment. The fundamental building blocks of any 3D scene are **primitive objects**. These are basic geometric shapes like spheres, cubes, cylinders, cones, planes, and tori, which serve as starting points for more complex models or as simple placeholders. You can create these primitives by navigating to `Create > Polygon Primitives` in the main menu. When you select one, it will appear at the origin (0,0,0) of your scene. It's good practice to immediately rename your objects to something descriptive in the Channel Box or Outliner (e.g., "GameCharacter_Body", "Environment_Wall_01") rather than leaving them as "pCube1", "pSphere1", etc. This habit will save you immense time and frustration as your scenes grow in complexity, especially in game development where clear asset naming is crucial for engine integration.

When you create an object in Maya, it's actually composed of two main parts: a **transform node** and a **shape node**. The transform node (e.g., `pCube1`) dictates the object's position, rotation, and scale in 3D space. It's what you interact with using the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools. The shape node (e.g., `pCubeShape1`) defines the actual geometry, its vertices, edges, and faces, as well as its material properties. While you usually interact with the transform node, understanding that the underlying geometry is separate is a key concept in Maya. This distinction allows for advanced operations like instancing or sharing geometry between multiple transform nodes.

As your scene grows, managing numerous objects becomes challenging without proper organization. This is where the **Outliner** becomes indispensable. Accessible via `Windows > Outliner`, this panel provides a hierarchical list of every item in your scene, including geometry, cameras, lights, and groups. It's your central hub for selecting, renaming, and understanding the relationships between objects. You can drag and drop objects within the Outliner to change their hierarchy, or double-click an object's name to rename it. A common mistake for beginners is to ignore the Outliner, leading to a cluttered scene where finding specific objects becomes a nightmare. Develop the habit of keeping your Outliner clean and organized from the very beginning.

A powerful way to organize objects and manage transformations collectively is through **grouping** and **parenting**.
**Parenting** creates a direct hierarchical relationship where one object (the child) inherits the transformations of another object (the parent). For example, if you parent a wheel to a car body, rotating or moving the car body will also rotate or move the wheel, but you can still move the wheel independently relative to the car. To parent, simply select the child object(s) first, then the parent object last, and press `P`. Alternatively, you can drag the child object onto the parent object within the Outliner.
**Grouping** is essentially creating an empty transform node (a "null" group) and making multiple objects children of that group. This is useful for logically organizing related objects without them being directly linked in a parent-child relationship to each other. For instance, you might group all the components of a house (walls, roof, windows) under a single "House_GRP" node. To group selected objects, press `Ctrl+G`. The pivot point of a newly created group will be at the average center of its children, or at the world origin if no objects are selected. It's often necessary to adjust the group's pivot point later. A common mistake is to group objects without considering the pivot point, which can lead to unexpected rotation or scaling behavior. Always check and adjust your pivot points (using the 'D' key) after grouping if the default isn't suitable.

For game development, maintaining a clean and logical scene hierarchy is paramount. Game engines rely heavily on this structure for animation, physics, and level design. A well-organized Maya scene translates directly into a more manageable and performant game asset. For example, when building a modular environment, you might group all assets belonging to a specific building type, then parent individual components (like doors or windows) to their respective wall sections. This progressive approach ensures that complex assets remain easy to edit and export.

screens.title: Understanding Scene Organization and Basic Objects
screens.subtitle: Create primitives, understand transform vs shape nodes, and organize your scene for reliable workflows.

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson we'll populate a blank Maya scene with basic primitives, and learn how the software represents each object as a transform and a shape. You will also build habits for naming and organizing objects using the Outliner, and learn grouping and parenting so complex assemblies behave predictably. These skills matter because every larger model, animation, or game asset begins with clear structure: a well-named, well-organized scene saves time when animating, exporting, or handing assets to a game engine. For example, creating a cube and immediately renaming it to Body avoids confusion later when you're exporting many pieces. We'll cover concrete steps: create primitives, rename them, inspect transform and shape nodes, establish parent-child relationships, and group assemblies into a single top-level node. Along the way I'll point out common mistakes such as leaving default names or grouping without checking pivot points. By the end you'll be able to assemble a simple character from primitives and organize it so it exports cleanly to a game or animation pipeline. Keep this orientation in mind as we move into hands-on steps and practical checks.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A Maya object is both a transform and a shape; naming, Outliner use, parenting, and grouping turn primitives into manageable assets.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: In this lesson you will practice four core skills that make scene building reliable and efficient. First, you will create and manipulate primitive 3D objects, which are the geometric starting points for modeling and placeholders during layout. Second, you will learn to differentiate transform nodes from shape nodes, so you understand where position and geometry live and why that separation matters when instancing or sharing geometry. Third, you will become comfortable using the Outliner to find, rename, and reorder objects; this is essential for keeping scenes navigable as they grow. Fourth, you will implement grouping and parenting to build logical hierarchies so complex assemblies move as intended. Each objective is paired with a small practice task and a visual mnemonic to reinforce the habit. Practically, these skills reduce export errors for games and keep animation rigs tidy. As you follow the guided lab, try to notice not only how to perform each action but why you would choose grouping versus parenting in a specific situation. By mastering these four objectives you’ll have a reproducible workflow for small to medium scene assemblies.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Habit
screens.subtitle: Tasks and habits that make scene organization repeatable

narration.text: Beyond knowing actions you should form reliable habits. This second objectives slide gives practical practice steps to cement the skills. First, immediately rename new primitives with descriptive names so you avoid sequences of default labels; doing this early prevents long searches later. Second, inspect every new object in the Outliner to confirm it has both a transform and a shape node; this helps you reason about where to place materials or where transforms come from. Third, practice parenting small assemblies so you can move complex parts by manipulating a single parent node while still adjusting children locally. Fourth, habitually group related components into a top-level group for export; group pivots must be checked to avoid surprising rotations. Each habit reduces friction during animation and export to a game engine. We'll practice these habits in the lab: build a simple three-piece character from primitives, parent the parts in sequence, then group them into one top-level node. These repeated small steps become the backbone of a professional scene-building workflow.

screens.title: Primitive Objects — Your Modeling Building Blocks
screens.subtitle: Cubes, spheres, cylinders, cones, planes, and tori as starting points and placeholders

narration.text: Primitives are the fundamental geometric shapes you create to begin modeling or block out a scene. In Maya these include the cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, plane, and torus. You create them from the menu path Create, Polygon Primitives, and each new primitive appears at the world origin by default. Think of primitives as clay blocks or placeholder props: they are quick to generate and can be refined into detailed models or remain as colliders and placeholders for layout. A good practice is to rename a new primitive immediately after creation. For example, when building a simple character start with a cube named Body, a sphere called Head, and a cylinder named Neck. This habit reduces search time later and makes collaborating with others or exporting to a game engine simpler. A common misconception is that primitives are temporary and need to be deleted; instead they are often the actual starting geometry for modeling. Try the hands-on step: create a cube, sphere, and cylinder and give each a clear descriptive name in the Outliner. Notice how this small action prevents later confusion and speeds iteration. What will you name your first primitive and why?

keyIdea.title: Primitive insight
keyIdea.text: Primitives are quick geometric bases or placeholders; rename them immediately to form a reliable scene vocabulary.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Primitive Objects
Definition
Primitive objects are basic polygonal shapes created as starting geometry or placeholders during scene layout. They appear at the origin and should be renamed immediately.
Common primitives
Cube, Sphere, Cylinder, Cone, Plane, Torus — each useful for different modeling goals or placeholder roles.
Practical tip
Rename freshly created primitives in the Outliner or Channel Box to descriptive names like Body, Head, or Neck to avoid later confusion.
Hands-on example
Create a cube, a sphere, and a cylinder. Rename them to Body, Head, and Neck to simulate character parts. Observe they appear in the Outliner with those names.
Example
In a blank scene create: Cube → rename Body; Sphere → rename Head; Cylinder → rename Neck. These three form the simple character core.
Common mistake
Leaving default names like pCube1 makes selection and export confusing as scenes grow. Avoid this by renaming immediately.
Key Takeaway

Treat primitives as intentional geometry or placeholders and name them clearly to support future edits and exports.

screens.title: Transform Node vs Shape Node
screens.subtitle: Why Maya separates transforms from geometry and how that affects your workflow

narration.text: Maya represents each visible object as at least two linked nodes: a transform node and a shape node. The transform node holds attributes for position, rotation, and scale — the values you change when you use the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools. The shape node contains the mesh data itself: vertices, edges, faces, and material assignments. This separation is purposeful: you can have multiple transform nodes reference the same shape data or swap shapes beneath a single transform. In practice this enables instancing and efficient memory use. For example, you might duplicate a tree transform many times while sharing a single tree shape to save resources. A common confusion for beginners is trying to apply a material to the transform instead of the shape; materials belong to the shape node. When you inspect the Outliner you will often see entries like pCube1 and pCubeShape1; the first is the transform, the second is the shape. When parenting or grouping, remember transforms determine hierarchical motion while shapes remain the visual geometry. Try selecting the transform to move the object and expand it in the Outliner to see the nested shape node. That simple inspection clarifies where changes to position versus geometry should be applied.

keyIdea.title: Node separation
keyIdea.text: Transforms control placement and motion; shapes store geometry and materials. Understanding both avoids selection and shading mistakes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Transform vs Shape
Claim
Every polygonal object in Maya consists of a transform node (position, rotation, scale) and a shape node (geometry and material). They are separate, linked objects in the scene graph.
Transform node
Holds translate, rotate, and scale values manipulated by tools. Parenting and grouping affect transforms.
Shape node
Holds mesh data and material assignments. Materials attach to the shape, not to the transform.
Concrete example
Create a sphere. In the Outliner you will see pSphere1 and pSphereShape1. Select pSphere1 and move it. The shape follows because transforms control placement. Select the shape to change material or geometry.
Misconception
Applying a texture to the transform has no effect. Materials must be applied to the shape node which owns geometry data.
Key Takeaway

Know which node holds transforms and which holds geometry so you edit the correct attributes and avoid wasted steps.

screens.title: Creating and Renaming Primitives — A Quick Workflow
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step: create objects, position them, and assign meaningful names

narration.text: Follow a short, repeatable process when adding primitives to a scene. Step one: create the primitives using Create, Polygon Primitives, and pick the shapes you need. Each new object appears at the origin. Step two: immediately rename the transform node in the Outliner or Channel Box to a descriptive name like Body, Head, or Environment_Wall_01. This habit saves time when scenes contain dozens or hundreds of items. Step three: position and orient using the Move and Rotate tools; remember these act on the transform node. Step four: check the Outliner to confirm the shape node is present and, if you plan to apply materials, select the shape node to do so. Step five: group or parent as required once a small assembly is complete. A common mistake is to delay renaming, which results in names like pCube3 that are hard to search and may break export conventions. Practice the sequence until it becomes second nature: create, rename, position, inspect shape, then organize. Creating and Renaming Primitives — A Quick Workflow means create → rename → position → inspect shape → organize. repetition of this flow prevents downstream confusion.. In practical terms, step-by-step: create objects, position them, and assign meaningful names. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable sequence
keyIdea.text: Create → Rename → Position → Inspect shape → Organize. Repetition of this flow prevents downstream confusion.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Create & Rename Workflow
Five-step process
1. Create
Use Create > Polygon Primitives to place new geometry at the origin.
2. Rename
Rename the transform node right away in the Outliner or Channel Box with a descriptive label.
3. Position
Move and rotate the transform to place the primitive in the scene where you need it.
4. Inspect shape
Confirm the shape node exists so you can apply materials or edit geometry when necessary.
5. Organize
Group or parent the object once it belongs to a larger assembly.
Example task
Create three primitives: cube, sphere, cylinder. Rename them Body, Head, Neck. Move the Head above the Neck and the Neck above the Body so they visually stack. Inspect the Outliner to see pCube1 and pCubeShape1 entries reflected by your renames.
Check your understanding
What happens if you rename only the shape node but not the transform? You may still see the default transform name appear in selection lists and export utilities.

screens.title: Using the Outliner to Manage Scene Hierarchy
screens.subtitle: Select, rename, reorder, and inspect relationships for clear scene structure

narration.text: The Outliner is Maya’s hierarchy browser showing every item in the scene. It lists transforms, shapes, lights, cameras, and groups in a tree so you can understand relationships at a glance. Use it to select objects, rename them, drag them into new parents, and quickly isolate parts of an assembly. A good Outliner practice is to maintain readable, hierarchical names and to intentionally create top-level groups for major assets. For example, group all parts of a building under Building_A_GRP and individual windows under Window_GRP inside that group. When you drag an object onto another in the Outliner you change its parent — this is equivalent to using the parenting hotkey. A common beginner mistake is ignoring the Outliner and relying on viewport selection alone; that leads to lost or hidden objects and confusing scene graphs. Practice: open Windows, Outliner, double-click a name to rename, and drag Head under Neck and Neck under Body to establish a Body → Neck → Head hierarchy. The Outliner will then clearly show that moving Body affects the whole sub-tree. This visual confirmation is the key value of the Outliner.

keyIdea.title: Outliner value
keyIdea.text: The Outliner visually exposes hierarchy and relationships, enabling precise renaming, selection, and parenting by drag-and-drop.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Outliner
Outliner — hierarchy and control
What it shows
A tree of transforms, shapes, cameras, lights, and groups. You can expand nodes to inspect child items and their shape nodes.
Key actions
  • Double-click a name to rename
  • Drag items to change parent-child relationships
  • Select items for precise transforms and edits
Practical example
After creating Body, Neck, Head, drag Head onto Neck and Neck onto Body in the Outliner. The resulting tree shows Body → Neck → Head and confirms how transforms will propagate when the Body moves.
Common mistake
Relying only on viewport selection can cause hidden items to remain unselected or mis-parented; the Outliner gives an authoritative view of scene structure.
Key Takeaway

Use the Outliner continuously as you build. It keeps your scene readable and makes hierarchy changes predictable and reversible.

screens.title: Parenting — Build Logical Transform Relationships
screens.subtitle: How parenting makes child objects inherit transformations from parents

narration.text: Parenting creates a direct transform inheritance: the child object inherits translation, rotation, and scale from its parent while keeping its own local transform. A classic example is a wheel parented to a car body; moving or rotating the car body carries the wheel along, but rotating the wheel locally still works. To parent in Maya, select the child or children first, then select the parent last and press P. Alternatively, drag the child onto the parent in the Outliner. A beginner trap is parenting in the wrong order, which produces the opposite hierarchy than intended. Another issue is assuming parenting changes geometry — it does not; only transforms are inherited. Parenting is expressive: you can parent multiple children to a single parent or create deeper hierarchies where transforms accumulate down the chain. Practice by selecting Head then Neck then Body with the hotkey method to build a Body → Neck → Head chain. Afterwards, move the Body and notice Neck and Head follow, then rotate the Neck to see the Head respond while the Body remains static. This hands-on experiment illustrates how parenting simplifies controlling assemblies during animation and export.

keyIdea.title: Parenting principle
keyIdea.text: Parenting links transforms so children inherit motion from parents while retaining local control for detailed edits.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Parenting
Parenting — how transforms propagate
How to parent
Select child(ren) first, then the parent and press P. Or drag child onto parent in the Outliner to change hierarchy.
Example: Head and Neck
Parent Head to Neck, then Neck to Body to create a chain where Body controls broad motion and Neck and Head respond locally.
Common mistake
Selecting parent before child creates the reverse relation. Verify the Outliner to confirm hierarchy after parenting.
Practice task
Select Head, then Neck, then Body and press P. Move Body to see the whole assembly move. Rotate Neck to see Head rotate with it. This confirms inheritance behavior.
Key Takeaway

Parenting builds predictable motion chains: parents control global motion, children keep local control.

screens.title: Grouping — Create Logical Collections
screens.subtitle: Use groups to collect related objects under a null transform for collective operations

narration.text: Grouping creates a new empty transform node and makes selected objects its children. This is useful when you want to manage a set of objects together without implying a parent-child functional relationship between those objects. For example, group all roof components under Roof_GRP or collect all props for a room under RoomA_GRP. To group press Control+G and then rename the generated group node to something meaningful. The pivot of the group is by default at the average center of its children, or at world origin if nothing was selected; you may need to adjust the pivot with the pivot tool. A common beginner mistake is grouping without checking the pivot, which can cause unexpected rotation or scaling behavior when that group is transformed later. Grouping also makes it simpler to export a collection as a single unit to a game engine. Practice by selecting Body, Neck, and Head and pressing Control+G, then rename the new node SimpleCharacter_GRP. After grouping, test rotating the group and observe how members move together. This pattern keeps assets modular and easier to manage. Grouping — Create Logical Collections means groups provide a neutral parent for collective transforms and exports; always check and set the group's pivot after creation.. In practical terms, use groups to collect related objects under a null transform for collective operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Grouping advantage
keyIdea.text: Groups provide a neutral parent for collective transforms and exports; always check and set the group's pivot after creation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Grouping
Grouping — when and how to use it
What grouping does
Creates an empty transform node that becomes the parent for selected objects, enabling collective operations without altering the internal parent-child relationships of those objects.
How to group
Select objects and press Control+G, then rename the group node. Adjust the pivot if necessary with the pivot tool before transforming.
Example
Select Body, Neck, Head, press Control+G to create SimpleCharacter_GRP. Rotate the group to move the assembly together; adjust pivot if rotation looks off.
Common mistake
Grouping without setting the pivot can lead to awkward rotations. Always check and set the pivot after grouping if the default center is not suitable.
Key Takeaway

Use groups to collect related items for export and scene management, and correct pivots to avoid transformation surprises.

screens.title: When to Parent vs When to Group
screens.subtitle: Understanding functional differences and choosing the right approach for your asset

narration.text: Parenting and grouping are both ways to organize objects, but they serve different purposes and convey different relationships. Parenting establishes a functional, inheritable relationship: the child truly depends on the parent for transforms. Use parenting when parts must move relative to a master part, like wheels attached to an axle or a hand attached to an arm. Grouping creates a neutral container that collects items for collective transforms and export without implying that the children are functionally subordinate. Group when you want to move a set of unrelated objects together or when preparing an asset for export. A common beginner confusion is using grouping when parenting is intended; that can make animation awkward because children are not linked logically. Conversely, parenting everything can create unnecessarily deep hierarchies that complicate edits. The practical rule: use parenting to express mechanical or anatomical relationships, and use grouping as a packaging or export tool. Try the example: parent wheels to car body to get functional motion, then group the whole car under Car_GRP for export. This pattern keeps internal behavior expressive while preserving a clean export container.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Parent for functional dependency and motion inheritance; group for packaging and export without changing internal relationships.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Parent vs Group
Comparison: Parenting vs Grouping
Parenting
  • Creates inheritance of transforms
  • Used for mechanical or anatomical relationships
  • Children keep local transforms while following parent
Grouping
  • Creates a neutral parent for collective operations
  • Useful for packaging and export
  • Pivot often needs adjustment after grouping
Example workflow
Parent logical components (wheels → axle → chassis). Then group the entire assembly under Car_GRP for export. This maintains functional relationships internally while packaging the whole asset for transfer.
Key Takeaway

Choose parenting when behavior is important. Choose grouping when you need a packaging container without implying internal dependence.

screens.title: Hands-on Lab: Build a Simple Character
screens.subtitle: Create primitives, rename them, parent them, and group the assembly

narration.text: This lab walks you through creating a simple three-piece character using primitives. Start with a blank scene. Step one: create a cube, sphere, and cylinder using the polygon primitives menu. Step two: rename the transform nodes in the Outliner to Body, Head, and Neck respectively. Step three: position the Head above the Neck and the Neck above the Body using the Move tool. Step four: establish hierarchy by parenting Head to Neck and Neck to Body using the P key or by dragging in the Outliner. Confirm the hierarchy reads Body → Neck → Head in the Outliner. Step five: test by moving Body and observing that Neck and Head follow. Step six: select all three and press Control+G to create SimpleCharacter_GRP and rename the group. Finally, check the group's pivot and adjust it with the pivot tool if rotation looks off. A common pitfall is parenting or grouping in the wrong order; always confirm the Outliner after each operation. This lab simulates a real pipeline practice and reinforces the sequence of create, rename, parent, and group for exportable assets.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: A reusable SimpleCharacter_GRP built from primitives, with a clear Body → Neck → Head hierarchy and corrected group pivot.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hands-on Lab
Lab walkthrough
Steps
  1. Create a cube, sphere, and cylinder from Create > Polygon Primitives.
  2. Rename transforms to Body, Head, Neck in the Outliner.
  3. Position Head above Neck and Neck above Body using Move.
  4. Parent Head to Neck and Neck to Body using P or drag in the Outliner.
  5. Select all and press Control+G to create SimpleCharacter_GRP and rename it.
  6. Adjust the group's pivot if rotation behaves unexpectedly.
Common checks
  • Does the Outliner show Body → Neck → Head?
  • Do materials apply to shape nodes rather than transforms?
  • Is the group pivot centered appropriately for rotation?
Scenario
You are preparing a character for a game engine. Build and organize the simple character so it exports as a single group and retains local motion for head and neck during animation.
Key Takeaway

This lab reinforces the create → name → parent → group sequence that keeps assets clear and engine-friendly.

screens.title: Naming Conventions and Scene Hygiene
screens.subtitle: Why descriptive naming and Outliner cleanliness pay off

narration.text: Good naming conventions are a small habit with large benefits. Use clear, consistent prefixes or patterns such as AssetName_Part or Environment_Wall_01 so teammates and export tools can find items predictably. Avoid leaving default names like pCube1 which offer no context. Keep scene hygiene by deleting unused nodes, organizing layers or groups, and using top-level groups for exportable assets. A clean Outliner also reduces mistakes when rigging, animating, or exporting: if a texture lookup or script expects a node named GameCharacter_Body, inconsistent naming breaks that pipeline. A common misconception is that renaming is optional; in collaborative and engine workflows it is essential. Practical rules: be descriptive but concise, use underscores or camelCase consistently, and include version or instance numbers when multiple similar assets exist. For practice, rename three primitives to Body_v01, Head_v01, Neck_v01 and create a SimpleCharacter_GRP. Then export only the group node; a clean naming scheme makes spotting missing pieces trivial. Good naming saves hours as projects scale. Naming Conventions and Scene Hygiene means adopt clear, consistent names and maintain outliner hygiene to avoid pipeline and export errors as scenes scale.. In practical terms, why descriptive naming and outliner cleanliness pay off. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Naming rule
keyIdea.text: Adopt clear, consistent names and maintain Outliner hygiene to avoid pipeline and export errors as scenes scale.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Naming & Hygiene
Naming conventions and scene hygiene
Why naming matters
Consistent names enable easy selection, scripting, and engine integration. They also reduce errors during export because tools often rely on predictable names.
Practical patterns
  • Use Asset_Part format like Car_Body or House_Window_01
  • Use underscores or camelCase consistently
  • Include version or instance numbers when appropriate
Practice task
Rename Body, Head, Neck to Body_v01, Head_v01, Neck_v01 and group them into SimpleCharacter_GRP. This makes it obvious which items belong to the asset when preparing exports.
Key Takeaway

Naming and tidying the Outliner early prevents confusion later and enables robust pipelines for animation and game export.

screens.title: Testing Hierarchies and Transform Propagation
screens.subtitle: Simple checks to confirm parenting and grouping behave as intended

narration.text: After you build a hierarchy or group an assembly, test it to ensure transforms propagate as expected. First, select the top-level parent or group and move it across the workspace; all children should move identically. Second, rotate the parent and verify children rotate together. Third, select a single child and rotate or move it locally to confirm it retains independent control relative to its parent. If any child does not follow the parent, check whether it was properly parented or grouped. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, primitive objects are your modeling starting points and placeholders; create and rename them immediately to support later work. Second, every visible object has a transform node that controls position, rotation, and scale, and a shape node that holds geometry and materials; edit the correct node for the intended effect. Third, the Outliner is your authoritative scene map; use it for renaming, reparenting, and confirming hierarchy. These concepts are the foundation of a tidy, export-ready scene and will make animation and game export far smoother. As you practice, emphasize consistent naming, test your hierarchy after parenting or grouping, and adjust pivots when needed. A clear scene structure prevents many downstream problems and is a hallmark of professional asset preparation. Keep these three ideas in mind as you create larger models and build more complex scenes.
